Two Firms Watching Each Other

In a town with only two cola firms, each firm sizes up the other and picks its output. The price is set by the two firms' combined output. Once the rival picks a quantity, a reply rule gives your best answer. The market settles where the two replies cross. That reply rule is the formula below. For example, only two booths sell 🍬 candy at the school fair. If the other booth puts out 10 📦 boxes, your share shrinks. If it puts out fewer boxes, you can add more without sinking the price.

P=a−b(q1+q2)P = a - b(q_1 + q_2)P=a−b(q1​+q2​)
q1=a−c−bq22bq_1 = \frac{a - c - b q_2}{2b}q1​=2ba−c−bq2​​

Examples & Exercises

Only two cola firms exist. The market price is P=12−(q1+q2)P = 12 - (q_1 + q_2)P=12−(q1​+q2​) and a bottle costs 333 to make. If firm 2 produces 333, what is firm 1's best move — and why do both stop there?

Show proof
  1. Firm 1's reply rule is q1=12−3−q22q_1 = \frac{12 - 3 - q_2}{2}q1​=212−3−q2​​. Plugging in q2=3q_2 = 3q2​=3 gives q1=3q_1 = 3q1​=3 — matching the rival is best.
  2. The total is 666 and the price is P=12−6=6P = 12 - 6 = 6P=12−6=6. Checking firm 2's reply rule at this point also gives q2=3q_2 = 3q2​=3 — each is answering the other perfectly, so nobody wants to move. That is the Cournot equilibrium.

In the same market, firm 2 suddenly floods production up to 666. How should firm 1 respond, and what happens to the market?

Show proof
  1. The reply rule with q2=6q_2 = 6q2​=6 gives q1=12−3−62=1.5q_1 = \frac{12 - 3 - 6}{2} = 1.5q1​=212−3−6​=1.5. When the rival floods the market, pulling back is best — insisting on the old quantity would crash the price further.
  2. Even so, the total rises to 7.57.57.5 and the price falls to 4.54.54.5. Firm 1's profit is (4.5−3)×1.5=2.25(4.5 - 3) \times 1.5 = 2.25(4.5−3)×1.5=2.25 — miserable next to the 999 it earned at the equilibrium. Losing the watching game is expensive.
